Preconditions: Create a NEW, disposable template (do not use a real school's live TC/bonafide/character template). Design it, render a proof, then publish it so publishedVersion=6 is not required — publish it once so publishedVersion=1. Record the SHA-256 hash of the v1 proof PDF via version_pdf before starting.
Steps: 1. Note the hash of the v1 PDF served by version_pdf(id,1,lang). 2. Call save(id,{version:1},lockVersion) — i.e. reset the mutable version counter back to the already-published number, changing no other field. 3. Edit the design (add or move one visible object) and save again if needed so the live head differs from what was frozen. 4. Call proof_pdf(id) to render the current (edited) design. 5. As any view-grade user, call version_pdf(id,1,lang) again and hash the bytes.
Input: version:1 in step 2; a visible design edit in step 3
Expected Result: The v1 PDF served in step 5 is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the hash captured before step 2 — it must NOT reflect the step-3 edit. If the hash differs, the 'a published version's certificate can never change' guarantee is broken by an edit-grade user with no manage grade and no race.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_template_service.php:335-339 (save()'s strip list omits `version`), Doc_templates.php:826,839,857-860 (proof_pdf() keys the on-disk filename to the live head's `version`, with no publishedVersion/activeVersion comparison, and writes unconditionally)
Invariant Defended: U1 / N2 — a published version is never rewritten
Risk: The single most severe finding this run: the artefact a school or auditor actually downloads for an 'immutable' certificate version is silently rewritable by an edit-grade staff member, deterministically, in two ordinary POSTs, no race required.
Remarks: RUN FIRST, on a disposable template only — never on a real school's active TC/bonafide/character template. QA-LEAD rules this P0 (A11 rated P1 and asked for P0 review).

Role: Staff — manage, then whoever reviews audit records
Preconditions: Complete T0-01 first (or a fresh repeat of it) so a published version's on-disk proof PDF has been overwritten.
Steps: 1. After reproducing T0-01, check the template's audit log (log_audit / AUDIT_MODULE=DocTemplates) for any entry describing the version-1 proof re-render. 2. Check get_versions(id) — does anything on the version-1 snapshot record (proofPdfHash, lastProof, or similar) change, or does it still show the ORIGINAL hash while the file on disk no longer matches it? 3. Check whether any UI surface (version history, gallery row, a warning banner) shows any indication that v1's proof file was touched after publication.
Expected Result: State plainly what a school would actually see: does ANYTHING — audit log, a hash-mismatch flag, a UI warning — notice that the frozen file no longer matches its own recorded hash? If the answer is 'nothing does', record that as its own finding: the tamper is not just possible, it is invisible.
Expectation Source: Requirement-derived — no code path found this run that compares a version snapshot's recorded hash against the live bytes on disk at read time
Evidence: _arbitration.md OV1 (QA-LEAD's own framing: 'the snapshot is honest and the artefact still changed')
Invariant Defended: N2 / N4 — a published version's record should be tamper-evident even if not tamper-proof
Risk: A silent, undetected tamper of a legal-record artefact is strictly worse than a detected one — this row measures which one we actually have.
Remarks: Depends on T0-01. If T0-01 could not be executed, mark this BLOCKED too.

Preconditions: A staff account on a school gated OUT of at least one statutory type (e.g. a Madhya Pradesh school; target type `study` is Andhra-Pradesh-only, requiresState). A disposable custom-type template.
Steps: 1. Confirm the baseline refusal: call create('study', {...}) directly and confirm it is refused ('...is not a document type this school can create'). 2. Create a custom-type template instead: create('custom:qa_state_gate_probe', {docTitle:'QA probe'}). Design it minimally. 3. Render a proof: proof_pdf(id). 4. Call save(id, {docType:'study'}, lockVersion) — do NOT touch page/header/footer/objects/languages/defaultLanguage. 5. Call publish(id). 6. Read the resulting documentTemplateVersions/{id}_v1 document directly (via get_versions or a Firestore read) and check its docType field. 7. Open the published version's proof/preview and check whether the render fails loudly (an unresolved-field error) or silently renders using the wrong type's layout.
Input: docType:'study' patched onto a custom-type template after proofing
Expected Result: publish() should REFUSE — a school not entitled to create a type must not be able to freeze a permanent record under that type. If it does not refuse: the frozen snapshot's docType field should NOT read 'study', or, if it does, the resulting render should fail loudly rather than silently mis-binding content designed for one contract into another's layout.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_template_service.php:372-382 (contentHash() omits docType), :527 (snapshot copies docType from the live head unchecked); Doc_templates.php:1095-1114,606 (_safe_type() is never called from save() or publish())
Invariant Defended: N4 (proof gate) / N9 (strip-list should be exhaustive) / the state-gating design itself
Risk: A state-gate bypass becomes a PERMANENT, undeletable record (delete() refuses once publishedVersion is set, and no unpublish/amend method exists anywhere) — escalates L9 from a reversible draft-only bug to a permanent one.
Remarks: Use ONLY a disposable custom-type template created for this test. QA-LEAD escalated this to P1. Subsumes A11-M1-08's render-mismatch check as step 7.

Preconditions: A staff account on a state-gated school as in T0-03. A disposable custom-type template, no proof required.
Steps: 1. Create a custom-type template: create('custom:qa_regression_probe', {docTitle:'QA regression probe'}). 2. Call save(id, {docType:'study'}, lockVersion) directly, without ever proofing or publishing. 3. Re-read the stored document and check its docType field.
Input: docType:'study' patched via save() on a fresh, never-proofed custom template
Expected Result: save() should REFUSE the docType change, the same way create('study',...) already refuses — a business-rule gate that is enforced at creation must be enforced everywhere the same field can be set. If it is not refused, docType must read the ORIGINAL custom:* value, not 'study'.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — _live-state.md L9, reproduced E4 by QA-LEAD 2026-09-04 against SCH_B56BB9A401 (population 85 before and after, no residue)
Risk: Already reproduced once (E4) and then deliberately deleted. This row exists to CONFIRM the fix later and guard against regression — do not skip it once a fix ships.
Remarks: This is the P2-reproduced baseline finding QA-LEAD's assignment specifically calls out; kept separate from T0-03 because T0-03 tests the WORSE consequence (surviving publish), this tests the underlying bypass itself.

Role: Staff — edit, PLUS the human's explicit authorisation before step 4
Preconditions: A disposable template. A host the HUMAN CONTROLS and can read the access log of (e.g. a webhook.site / requestbin endpoint the human owns, or a personal server) — NEVER a third party's domain, NEVER the production AWS metadata address.
Steps: 1. On the disposable template, set an object's style.fontFamily to: Arial;background:url(<HUMAN-CONTROLLED-HOST>/qa-ssrf-probe). 2. Call preview() and confirm in the browser network tab whether a request to <HUMAN-CONTROLLED-HOST> fires from the ADMIN'S OWN BROWSER (this part is safe — it is your own browser making the request, not the server). 3. STOP AND GET EXPLICIT HUMAN AUTHORISATION before this step. Only once authorised: call proof_pdf(id) against the SAME template, then check the human-controlled host's access log for a hit ORIGINATING FROM THE PRODUCTION OHIO SERVER (not your browser) in the same time window.
Expected Result: Step 2 (browser preview) is expected to fire — the injection is already confirmed at E3. Step 4's result is the open question: if the human-controlled host's log shows a hit from the PRODUCTION SERVER's IP, mPDF is dereferencing the URL server-side and this is confirmed server-side SSRF (rate P0 — the same technique could target the AWS instance-metadata address 169.254.169.254). If no server-originated hit appears, the risk is limited to the already-confirmed browser-side beacon (rate P2).
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_serializer.php:474,477 (style.fontFamily/track escaped with htmlspecialchars(), wrong for a CSS-attribute context), Doc_renderer.php:391 (guardImages() only scans , never style= attributes or url())
Invariant Defended: The one control (guardImages()) purpose-built against exactly this SSRF threat model
Risk: P1 confirmed injection; P0 IF mPDF dereferences server-side and the instance can reach the metadata endpoint; P2 if it does not dereference at all. The single highest-value untested row in this entire certification.
Remarks: HARD GATE (H4): do not run step 4 without the human's explicit, in-the-moment authorisation, and NEVER point it at a third party or at 169.254.169.254 itself — use a host you own and can read the log of. Steps 1-2 (browser-only) may be run without that authorisation since no production server is touched.

Role: Staff — manage, with the ability to interrupt a request mid-flight (proxy/devtools throttling or engineering support)
Preconditions: A disposable, proofed draft, ready to publish. A way to interrupt the connection between the two writes inside publish() — e.g. Chrome DevTools 'offline' toggled at the right instant, or a network proxy that can be killed on command.
Steps: 1. Begin publish(id). 2. Attempt to cut the connection AFTER the documentTemplateVersions snapshot write lands but BEFORE the documentTemplates head update (publishedVersion/version bump) completes — this is a narrow window and may take several attempts. 3. If successfully stranded: retry publish(id) on the same template and observe the response. 4. Check whether the orphaned documentTemplateVersions/{id}_v{n} snapshot exists with no corresponding head pointer.
Input: A killed connection timed to land between publish()'s write #1 and write #2
Expected Result: The template enters the STRANDED state: the orphaned snapshot exists and is correct, but every retry of publish() refuses with 'already exists' — and there is no designed, self-service repair. Confirm both halves: the orphan exists, AND the retry is permanently refused, not merely delayed.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_template_service.php:514-522,551,563 (set() then update(), no commit wrapping them; the exists() guard then blocks every retry forever)
Invariant Defended: Availability of the publish lifecycle for that template, permanently
Risk: Two independent code traces (A4, A5) already agree this is the shape; this row is what would confirm it actually strands a template on the real network, not just in theory.
Remarks: Hard to hit the exact timing window without engineering support (a breakpoint or fault-injection proxy) — likely BLOCKED for a non-technical tester; flag accordingly and consider a dev-assisted repro instead. Re-run mandatory after AR1/T0-01's fix ships, since that fix removes the accidental version-bump escape (T0-07).

Role: Staff — edit, engineering support to first induce STRANDED (depends on T0-06)
Preconditions: A template successfully stranded via T0-06 (or a non-production copy of the environment where this can be induced safely).
Steps: 1. On the stranded template, call save(id, {version: N+1}, lockVersion) where N is the stuck version number. 2. Attempt publish(id) again. 3. Inspect the resulting head document: is publishedVersion now correct and pointing at a real, non-stale snapshot? Or does the template merely become publishable again while publishedVersion is left stale relative to the orphaned snapshot from T0-06?
Input: version: N+1 patched directly onto the stranded head
Expected Result: Document the ACTUAL outcome precisely — this determines whether the OV1/T0-01 fix (stripping `version` from save()'s patch list) can ship alone, or whether it must ship together with a real repair tool. Either a full, correct repair, or a partial unblock with a stale publishedVersion, is an acceptable finding here — but it must be established, not assumed.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — 02-state-machine.md §4 I-10, §6 (the only known STRANDED escape, and an undesigned one)
Invariant Defended: R-2 (no designed recovery from a stranded publish)
Risk: Determines whether fixing T0-01 (a P0) accidentally removes the only known way out of a P1 stuck state, breaking recovery for anyone already stranded when the fix ships.
Remarks: Depends on T0-06. Run in a non-production copy if at all possible — this deliberately induces a stuck, difficult-to-clean state.

Role: Human with AWS Lightsail console access (not app-testable)
Preconditions: Access to the AWS Lightsail console for the Ohio (us-east-2) production instance, or documented knowledge of its backup configuration.
Steps: 1. In the Lightsail console, check whether automatic/manual snapshots are configured for the instance. 2. Confirm whether `uploads/` (specifically `uploads/{schoolId}/doctemplates/_proofs/`) is included in whatever backup mechanism exists — instance snapshots capture the whole disk, but confirm no exclusion is configured. 3. If comfortable doing so in a non-production context, perform a restore drill from the most recent snapshot and confirm a known proof PDF is present in the restored copy.
Expected Result: State plainly whether the record of every historical published certificate PDF would survive an instance loss or migration. If snapshots do not cover `uploads/`, or none are configured at all, this is a live disaster-recovery gap for the one artefact whose entire purpose is to survive.
Expectation Source: Requirement-derived — PATH_A_US_SERVER_RUNBOOK.md:60-62,117 (uploads/ must be rsynced BY HAND on migration; not in git)
Invariant Defended: Durability of the published-version artefact — the module's own stated purpose
Risk: If the instance is lost or rebuilt without a manual rsync, version_pdf() 404s for every version ever published while Firestore still cheerfully lists them as published — a silent, total loss of the legal record with no error surfaced anywhere in the app.
Remarks: H1 — this is an infrastructure fact no amount of code reading can answer; not executable from within the app itself.

Preconditions: Two real schools in the same Firebase project, School A (the tester's own) and School B, with a REAL templateId belonging to School B (e.g. seeded specifically for this test, or an existing template if a second real tenant is already available).
Steps: As School A's authenticated session, call each of: get_template(School B's real id), get_versions(School B's real id), version_pdf(School B's real id, any version, any lang). Do not modify anything.

This is the difference between 'the check fires' and 'the id merely doesn't exist', which the E3 probe already run this pass (a NON-existent id) could not distinguish.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_template_service.php:888-900 (head()'s tenant check, its own comment: several lifecycle methods 'used to have no tenant check at all' before a refactor); Doc_templates.php:353,387,474-481
Invariant Defended: N7 — tenant isolation on every read; global invariant #1
Risk: The single largest standing [UNKNOWN] in the whole certification, per A11's own framing — every prior pass agrees this is genuinely unproven, not merely under-tested.
Remarks: BLOCKED without a real second-tenant template id — this is the H1/H2 fixture gap named by every prior agent. Prioritise obtaining or seeding this fixture over any other single item in this matrix.

Role: Staff — edit and manage grade, School A, PLUS a real second school's real template id
Preconditions: Same fixture as T0-09.
Steps: As School A's session, attempt each of: save(School B's id, {...}, anyLockVersion), publish(School B's id), activate(School B's id), deactivate(School B's id), delete(School B's id), archive(School B's id). Confirm none applies any change to School B's data.
Input: School B's real templateId, School A's session, harmless patch bodies
Expected Result: Every call refuses, identically to how it refuses against a non-existent id, with NO write applied to School B's document (verify with a follow-up read as School B, or via console, that nothing changed).
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — same head()-gated code path as T0-09, applied to the write-side lifecycle methods

Role: Two staff sessions with scripting ability (or two people counting down to click Save simultaneously), same template, same lockVersion
Preconditions: Both sessions have loaded the same template and hold the identical lockVersion.
Steps: Fire both sessions' save() calls as close to simultaneously as tooling allows (parallel scripted HTTP requests are far more reliable than two people clicking), each with a DIFFERENT patch (e.g. Session A changes the header text, Session B changes the footer text).
Expected Result: Per the module's own doc-comment ('the loser gets a conflict; nobody gets a lost edit'), exactly ONE request should succeed and the other should be refused with a conflict (E_CONFLICT / 409), not silently overwritten. If BOTH succeed, one edit is silently lost.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_template_service.php:27-28 (doc-comment claims CAS), :314-332 (implementation is read-then-compare-in-PHP-then-unconditional-write, no Firestore precondition available on setDocument/updateDocument)
Invariant Defended: C1 — save()/create() claim CAS and implement read-then-write (CONTESTED, code cannot settle it)
Risk: This is the direct runtime test of the module's own central architectural weak point — the doc-comment's guarantee failing exactly as the static trace predicts would mean silent lost edits on what the product calls a legal record.
Remarks: Best run with two scripted parallel HTTP requests (curl/Postman with a shared timer), not two human clicks — human reaction time is unlikely to land inside the race window. This is the single highest-value concurrency row — it settles C1.

Role: Two staff sessions with scripting ability, same school
Preconditions: Both sessions on the hub, ready to create a new template of the same document type.
Steps: Fire both sessions' create() calls as close to simultaneously as tooling allows.
Input: Two simultaneous create() calls, same docType, same school
Expected Result: Two DISTINCT template ids (e.g. TPL0086, TPL0087) are minted — neither create silently overwrites the other. If both compute the same next-number and both pass their own exists() check before either write lands, the second write could silently annihilate the first template with no error.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_template_service.php:194,206,245 (unbounded numbering scan + create-only retry, a TOCTOU shape, not a real CAS)
Invariant Defended: Uniqueness of a newly-created template id
Risk: Same root architectural gap as T0-11 (C1), a different call site.
Remarks: Best run with two scripted parallel requests. Related to T0-11 — both exercise the same missing-precondition pattern.

Role: Two `manage` sessions with scripting ability, same proofed draft
Preconditions: A single proofed, unpublished draft, opened in two sessions.
Steps: Fire both sessions' publish() calls as close to simultaneously as tooling allows (scripted parallel requests — this subsumes the weaker rapid-double-click and network-throttled-double-click variants of the same test).
Input: Two simultaneous publish() calls on the same template
Expected Result: Exactly ONE version freezes cleanly. The loser receives a clean, specific refusal (e.g. 'already exists' or a conflict) — not a corrupted head where version/publishedVersion disagree with which snapshot document actually exists, and not two documentTemplateVersions documents for the same version number.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_template_service.php:514-522,551,563 (create-only exists() guard, two non-atomic writes)
Evidence: 05d-adversary-rows.md A11-M1-06, A11-M3-05, A11-M5-03 (merged into this one row — same assertion, escalating rigor)
Risk: A double-submit under real production latency could interleave publish()'s two non-atomic writes in an unintended order.
Remarks: Merges three adversary rows (A11-M1-06 sequential double-click, A11-M3-05 throttled double-click, A11-M5-03 scripted simultaneous) into the strongest single test — scripted parallel requests subsume the weaker variants.

Preconditions: Two DIFFERENT published templates of the SAME (school, docType) — e.g. two transfer-certificate templates, both with a publishedVersion.
Steps: Fire both sessions' activate() calls simultaneously, each activating a DIFFERENT one of the two templates.
Input: Two simultaneous activate() calls on sibling templates of the same docType
Expected Result: Exactly ONE template ends up with activeVersion set; the other's activeVersion is correctly nulled. This is the one place the module claims REAL atomicity (a Firestore commitBatch with a precondition) — confirm it holds under actual concurrency, not just by code trace.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_template_service.php:650-702 (single commitBatch naming the winner AND nulling every sibling's activeVersion in the same atomic write)
Evidence: 03-invariants.md N1; 05d-adversary-rows.md A11-M5-04 (also covers the narrower A11-M5-07 rollback-vs-forward-activate variant on the same template)
Invariant Defended: N1 — exactly one active template per (school, docType)
Risk: The one genuinely atomic write in the whole module deserves the same concurrency scrutiny as the seams that are known NOT to be atomic — a clean pass here is a real, valuable confirmation, not a formality.
Remarks: If time allows, repeat with both calls targeting the SAME template at two different versions (rollback vs forward) — A11-M5-07's narrower variant — instead of authoring it as a separate row.

Role: Two staff sessions from DIFFERENT schools, direct HTTP (no UI path exists for this endpoint)
Preconditions: Neither School A nor School B has yet created a reusableBlocks document with the id both are about to use (e.g. 'letterhead').
Steps: Both sessions POST save_block with the IDENTICAL blockId (e.g. 'letterhead') within the same narrow window, scripted via direct HTTP since this endpoint has zero UI callers.
Input: Identical blockId, different schoolId (forced server-side per session)
Expected Result: The LOSING school's client must be told it lost — a conflict response, not a silent HTTP 200. Per the code trace, today BOTH callers receive a clean success and the second write's schoolId silently wins, meaning one school's block is silently reassigned to the other tenant while its true owner is told 'Saved'.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_block_service.php:94-105 (no CAS; only refuses on an EXISTING doc with a DIFFERENT stored schoolId — a first-write race is entirely unguarded)
Invariant Defended: Tenant isolation on write; 'a write that reports success should not silently vanish'
Risk: A shared letterhead/seal/signature block silently reassigned to a different school's tenant, with the true owner's client showing 'Saved'.
Remarks: Requires direct HTTP scripting (no UI reaches save_block at all) and a second real tenant account — narrows the realistic attacker to a technical insider, but does not close the gap. BLOCKED without a second-tenant account.

Preconditions: A manage-grade session with access to the legacy /certificates dashboard (linked in the live sidebar today).
Steps: 1. Navigate to /certificates/generate (or the sidebar's 'Generate' entry). 2. Generate a certificate for a real or disposable test student, using a hardcoded type (bonafide/transfer/character/custom). 3. Confirm the action completes and note the certificate number issued and where the resulting record is stored (RTDB path). 4. Navigate to /certificates/issued and confirm the new record appears there.
Input: A test student's profile; one of the 4 hardcoded legacy document types
Expected Result: Establish, with direct observation, that this system DOES issue a real, student-identified document today — writing a complete issued record with a certificate number to RTDB — from a surface that is in the sidebar and has zero automated tests. This settles (with evidence, not inference) the C2/UR-6 question of whether the ecosystem issues certificates today.
Expectation Source: Requirement-derived — this is the IS/SHOULD question the code cannot settle on its own; the row exists to establish the IS with direct observation
Invariant Defended: ⚑ CONTESTED — which certificate system is authoritative
Risk: Reframes the whole certification's scope: if this is true, the ecosystem issues certificates today from an untested prototype, and the Document Engine's CON-NO_PRINT_IMPL constraint describes only half the truth.
Remarks: Use a DISPOSABLE test student profile, never a real enrolled student's record, for this probe.

Preconditions: Complete T0-16 (one legacy certificate issued, with its certificate number recorded). A Document Engine template published at least once (any disposable one from T0-01 will do).
Steps: 1. Record the legacy certificate number issued in T0-16. 2. Record the Document Engine's own version identifier for a published template (e.g. TPL0001_v1). 3. Check whether either system's numbering scheme has any awareness of, or reservation against, the other's numbers.
Input: n/a — comparison of two already-produced identifiers
Expected Result: Confirm, by direct comparison, that the two systems have ZERO numbering coordination — two independently-numbered 'official' certificate systems sharing one RBAC key ('Certificates'), with nothing preventing the same-looking serial from being minted twice under two different meanings.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Certificates.php:443-447 (legacy's own read-increment-write counter) vs. Doc_resolver's complete absence of any counter (N12, 03-invariants.md)
Invariant Defended: Ecosystem-level: one legal-record system should not silently duplicate certificate serials with another
Risk: Not a live collision today (the Document Engine issues nothing), but becomes one the moment any print point is wired — and nobody has designed against it.

Preconditions: A disposable template, NOT a live school's active certificate. Design it, render a proof, publish it as v1. Record the hash of v1's PDF.
Steps: 1. Publish v1, record its PDF hash via version_pdf. 2. Edit the LIVE DRAFT (which is now a new, unpublished v2-in-progress) with a clearly visible change (e.g. a large red banner). Save it, but do NOT publish it. 3. Re-download version 1's PDF via version_pdf(id,1,lang) and re-hash it.
Input: A visible edit to the draft AFTER v1 is published, without publishing that edit
Expected Result: The v1 PDF is UNCHANGED (same hash as step 1) — editing the running draft must never silently change what a previously published version renders. This is the module's most dangerous available failure mode if it occurred, and this row proves or disproves it directly on a controlled artefact (the live-state.md probe used a real production template and inferred this from a pre-existing edit; this row reproduces it cleanly).
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_template_service.php:529-536 (publish()'s snapshot is a plain in-process array copy, not a resolution step); Doc_serializer.php:482-571 (closed, fail-closed object-type switch — no block/blockRef reference type exists)
Evidence: 03-invariants.md N3 (self-containment, CONFIRMED structurally); _live-state.md L7 (E3, but on a live production template)
Invariant Defended: N3 / U1 — version snapshots are self-contained, not live pointers
Risk: If this failed, EVERY published certificate in the school would be silently mutable by editing the current draft — the module's own worst-case scenario.
Remarks: This is a controlled, repeatable version of the live-state.md L7 experiment — run it on a disposable template so it becomes a clean regression test rather than a one-off observation on TPL0001.

Preconditions: A disposable template published at least once (publishedVersion is not null).
Steps: Attempt delete(id) on the published template.
Expected Result: The delete is refused, with a message naming the reason (a published version is 'the record of what a certificate issued from it actually said') and, ideally, naming Archive as the remedy. The document must NOT be removed.
Expectation Source: Implementation-derived — Doc_template_service.php:799-806 (delete() refuses if publishedVersion≠null)
Invariant Defended: N5 — a template cannot be deleted once it has a published version
Risk: The one deletion guard that IS correctly enforced today — worth a direct confirmation since it anchors several other findings (e.g. why archive is the only remedy, and why the gallery only grows).
Remarks: Low risk, high value as a regression anchor for the several other T1/T2 rows about archive being the (UI-unreachable) remedy.
